questions.q: What does an RNN's hidden state represent?
options: A fixed set of learned weights shared across all layers
A running summary of everything the network has seen so far in the sequence
The final output prediction for the whole sequence
A copy of the input at the current timestep only
questions.explain: The hidden state is the only channel carrying information from earlier timesteps forward; it's a running summary updated at every step.

questions.q: In nn.RNN with batch_first=True, what shape is the input tensor expected to have?
options: (seq_len, batch, input_size)
(input_size, batch, seq_len)
(batch, seq_len, input_size)
(batch, input_size)
questions.explain: batch_first=True arranges tensors as (batch, seq_len, features) instead of PyTorch's default (seq_len, batch, features).

questions.q: What is the difference between nn.RNN's two return values, output and h_n?
options: output is the hidden state at every timestep; h_n is only the final timestep's hidden state
output is the loss; h_n is the prediction
They are identical and either can be used interchangeably
output is for training only; h_n is for inference only
questions.explain: output gives the hidden state produced at every position in the sequence; h_n is just the hidden state from the last timestep.

questions.q: Why can't an RNN parallelize computation across the sequence (time) dimension on a GPU?
options: GPUs don't support recurrent layers at all
Because hidden state h_t depends on h_{t-1}, creating a hard step-by-step dependency chain
Because nn.RNN only runs on CPU
Because sequence data is always too short to benefit from parallelism
questions.explain: Each timestep's hidden state requires the previous timestep's hidden state to already be computed, so the sequence dimension can't be spread across parallel compute.

questions.q: Why does an RNN reuse the same weights (W_ih, W_hh) at every timestep instead of learning separate weights per position?
options: To save disk space when saving the model
Because PyTorch doesn't allow per-timestep weights
So a fixed number of parameters can handle sequences of any length
Because separate weights per timestep would always perform worse
questions.explain: Sharing weights across timesteps is exactly what lets an RNN process variable-length sequences with a fixed, small parameter count.
